title: Chinese Braised Beef Brisket
subtitle: Lo shui brisket slow-braised in a spiced soy master stock
excerpt: Beef brisket braised low and slow in a fragrant master stock develops a deep, lacquered colour and fork-tender texture that no quick method can replicate. The stock improves with every use and can be frozen, then replenished. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Lo shui (master stock) braising is a Cantonese technique documented in Chinese culinary texts from the Song dynasty, used across roast shops and home kitchens throughout Guangdong and Hong Kong. The principle of maintaining and replenishing a single pot of spiced stock -- each batch enriching the next -- is one of the oldest continuous cooking traditions in Chinese cuisine.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze the brisket submerged in its braising stock for up to 3 months. Defrost overnight in the fridge and reheat gently in the stock.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The brisket improves overnight. Braise the day before, cool in the stock, refrigerate, and reheat sliced in the stock before serving.

content.text: This recipe serves 4 and takes about 2 hours 30 minutes -- most of it unattended. Beef brisket braised in a spiced
turns from a tough, fibrous cut into something that yields to a spoon, all while taking on a deep mahogany glaze from the soy and caramelised sugars in the braising liquid.

Do not rush the braise. The collagen in brisket needs sustained low heat to convert to gelatin -- if you simmer hard, the meat seizes before it can soften. Keep the liquid at a bare tremor: a bubble breaking the surface every few seconds is ideal. After braising, let the brisket cool in the stock so it reabsorbs moisture as the temperature drops.

Bring a large saucepan of water to the boil. Add the brisket pieces and blanch for 5 minutes, skimming any grey foam that rises. Drain, rinse the beef under cold water, and discard the blanching liquid. This cleans the meat and prevents a murky stock.
Return the saucepan to the hob. Add the 1 litre of fresh water, light soy sauce, the dark soy sauce, and Shaoxing wine. Stir in the sugar until dissolved.

Add the star anise, five spice, ginger, and garlic to the pot. Bring to the boil, then lower to a gentle simmer. Taste the stock -- it should be well-seasoned, savoury, and lightly sweet. Adjust with a pinch more sugar or soy if needed.

Add the blanched brisket pieces to the stock. The liquid should come at least two-thirds up the beef. Top up with water if not. Place a piece of baking paper directly on the surface of the liquid to keep the exposed beef moist.

Simmer gently for 2 hours, turning the beef once at the halfway point. The brisket is ready when a chopstick passes through the thickest part with no resistance and the surface looks lacquered and deep brown.
Remove the pot from the heat and let the brisket cool in the stock for at least 20 minutes. This is when it reabsorbs liquid. If serving later, refrigerate the brisket in the stock overnight.

To serve, lift the brisket out and slice against the grain into 1 cm pieces. Ladle a little of the warm braising stock over the top, drizzle with sesame oil, and scatter over sliced spring onions. Serve with steamed rice and extra braising stock on the side as a dipping sauce.

items.symptom: The brisket is still tough after 2 hours
items.cause: The simmer was too vigorous, or the cut was thicker than expected
items.fix: Continue braising in 30-minute increments, checking with a chopstick each time. Brisket from the flat end takes longer than the point end.

items.symptom: The stock is very pale and lacks depth
items.cause: Too little dark soy sauce, or the sugar was not caramelised first
items.fix: Add an extra 20 ml of dark soy sauce and simmer uncovered for 15 minutes to concentrate the stock.

items.symptom: The meat is dry after slicing
items.cause: The brisket was cooled outside the stock or sliced too early
items.fix: Always cool the meat in the braising liquid. Reheat sliced pieces in stock rather than in a dry pan.

content.text: Braised brisket (lo ngau lam) is a fixture in Hong Kong street stalls and roast shops, sold alongside soy-poached chicken and five-spice pork. The master stock concept -- a perpetually maintained braising liquid -- ties this dish to a broader Chinese tradition of lo shui cooking where the stock itself accumulates flavour over years of use. At home, the braising liquid can be strained, cooled, frozen, and reused repeatedly, growing richer with each batch.
